title: French Revolution Begins
summary: The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789 became the French Revolution's most enduring symbol, but the revolutionary rupture had already begun with the Estates-General, the National Assembly, and the Tennis Court Oath. Over the next decade, successive assemblies dismantled legal privilege, attempted constitutional monarchy, proclaimed a republic, fought civil and international wars, and governed through emergency measures during the Terror. Napoleon's coup of 1799 ended the Directory and is often treated as the close of the Revolution's republican phase, although revolutionary institutions and conflicts continued to shape France and Europe.

title: Ancien Régime Structure
summary: French society was legally organised around three orders: the clergy, the nobility, and the Third Estate, which included the overwhelming majority of the population. Privileges, taxes, offices, and seigneurial rights varied by province and status, and the Ancien Régime had changed considerably since the Middle Ages rather than remaining frozen in time. Even so, inherited legal distinctions and the political power of privileged bodies made comprehensive fiscal and constitutional reform exceptionally difficult.

title: Estates System Inequality
summary: The clergy and nobility formed a small minority of the population but controlled a substantial share of land, offices, and legal privileges. They were not wholly tax-free, and exemptions varied, yet the fiscal system generally assessed wealth and status unevenly. The Third Estate ranged from prosperous merchants and officeholders to artisans, labourers, and peasants, so it was not a single economic class. By the late 1780s, fiscal collapse and subsistence hardship turned these long-standing inequalities into a national political crisis.

title: Tax Burden on Commoners
summary: Many commoners paid the taille, indirect taxes such as the gabelle, seigneurial dues, Church tithes, and in some regions road-building corvée labour. Noble exemptions were extensive but not universal, while the clergy made negotiated payments to the crown rather than being entirely untaxed. Tax farming, venal offices, regional exceptions, and unequal assessment made revenue collection both inefficient and widely resented.

title: Growing Public Resentment
summary: Resentment grew from unequal taxation, seigneurial dues, food insecurity, restricted access to offices, and the conspicuous privileges of corporate bodies. Attitudes varied by class and region, and many critics initially sought reform rather than revolution. By 1788–1789, however, pamphlets, political clubs, the cahiers de doléances, and Enlightenment language helped turn diverse local grievances into arguments about representation, citizenship, and national sovereignty.

title: Enlightenment Ideas Spread
summary: Voltaire criticised religious intolerance and arbitrary authority, Montesquieu analysed mixed government and the division of political power, and Rousseau developed an influential account of popular sovereignty. Their works circulated through books, salons, academies, clandestine publications, and the Encyclopédie. Enlightenment thought did not provide a single revolutionary programme, but it supplied educated readers with competing languages of rights, reform, constitutionalism, and political legitimacy.

title: Questioning Royal Authority
summary: Divine-right monarchy and unqualified royal authority were increasingly challenged during the eighteenth century, although monarchy itself remained widely accepted in 1789. Many reformers wanted a constitutional king, representative institutions, and government under law rather than a republic. Louis XVI's inconsistent responses to the fiscal and political crisis gradually made royal authority appear contingent on the nation's consent rather than beyond public judgment.

title: Monarchy Financial Crisis
summary: By 1788, the French crown faced an acute credit and liquidity crisis. Servicing the accumulated debt absorbed more than half of ordinary royal revenue, while the tax system could not reliably reach privileged wealth or produce sufficient new income. War costs, administrative fragmentation, and failed reform attempts undermined confidence among lenders. When further borrowing became unavailable, the monarchy could no longer postpone a political settlement over taxation and representation.

title: War Debt Accumulation
summary: The Seven Years' War and France's intervention in the American War of Independence greatly enlarged the royal debt. The American conflict probably cost the crown around one billion livres, though estimates vary, and it was one major burden among many rather than the sole cause of bankruptcy. Its immediate significance was fiscal; the political influence of American independence on French officers and readers was real but more diffuse.

title: Inefficient Tax System
summary: Royal taxation was a patchwork of direct and indirect levies, provincial arrangements, exemptions, tax farms, and purchased offices. Some nobles paid taxes such as the capitation and vingtième, but assessment and enforcement were highly unequal. Reform threatened privileged landowners, officeholders, provincial institutions, and the parlements, all of which could obstruct change. The Assembly of Notables' refusal to endorse a universal land tax exposed the crown's inability to reform taxation without broader political consent.

title: Failed Tax Reforms
summary: Calonne proposed a broad territorial land tax and other reforms in 1786, then asked an Assembly of Notables to approve them in 1787. The Notables refused to grant the crown the authority it sought and demanded fuller accounts and representative sanction. Brienne's subsequent struggle with the parlements deepened the constitutional crisis. Necker's popular Compte rendu of 1781 had not revealed the true wartime deficit: by presenting ordinary revenue and expenditure while excluding much extraordinary borrowing, it made the finances appear healthier than they were. By 1788, summoning the Estates-General had become unavoidable.

title: Estates-General Convened
summary: The Estates-General opened at Versailles in May 1789, its first meeting since 1614. The Third Estate had received double representation, but the crucial voting procedure remained unresolved. Voting by order would allow the clergy and nobility to outvote the Third Estate two to one; voting by head could give the Third Estate and reform-minded allies a majority. The procedural deadlock quickly became a dispute over whether political authority belonged to the traditional orders or to the nation.

title: Third Estate Asserts Power
summary: After weeks of deadlock over verification and voting, deputies of the Third Estate invited members of the other orders to join them and on June 17, 1789 declared themselves the National Assembly. Some parish clergy soon joined. This claim to represent the French nation preceded the later lockout and Tennis Court Oath and transformed an institutional dispute inside the Estates-General into a challenge to the political basis of the monarchy.

title: Tennis Court Oath
summary: On June 20, 1789, after finding their usual meeting hall closed, deputies of the newly declared National Assembly gathered in a nearby indoor tennis court. They swore not to separate until France had a constitution; 576 of the 577 deputies present signed the oath. Whether the closure was a deliberate royal attempt to exclude them remains debated, but the oath publicly demonstrated the Assembly's unity and refusal to let the crown dissolve it.

title: National Assembly Formed
summary: On June 17, 1789, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, asserting that legitimate taxation and law required representation of the nation rather than separate corporate orders. After the Tennis Court Oath and the royal session of June 23, the deputies continued meeting despite royal pressure. Louis XVI ordered the remaining privileged deputies to join them on June 27. This did not immediately abolish monarchy, but it made restoration of unqualified royal sovereignty increasingly difficult.

title: Bread Shortages Crisis
summary: A poor harvest in 1788, followed by a severe winter and disrupted grain supplies, drove bread prices sharply upward in the spring and summer of 1789. Prices and wages varied, but poor urban households often spent most of their income on bread, leaving almost no margin when prices rose. Subsistence anxiety did not by itself cause the Revolution, but it intensified distrust of authorities and made political confrontation inseparable from the demand for food.

title: Financial Strain on People
summary: Many peasants, artisans, and urban labourers entered 1788 with little protection against a bad harvest, unemployment, taxes, rents, and seigneurial dues. Conditions differed sharply across France, and not every rural family was destitute, but indebtedness and underemployment were widespread. The food-price shock of 1789 therefore struck populations that often lacked savings or reliable relief, turning fiscal and constitutional conflict into an immediate social emergency.

title: Urban Unrest
summary: During the spring and summer of 1789, crowds attacked grain convoys, imposed prices in markets, and confronted local authorities in several parts of France. Paris became especially volatile as speakers at the Palais-Royal linked food scarcity to fears of royal repression. After Necker's dismissal became known on July 12, crowds searched for weapons, clashed with troops, and created a revolutionary municipal authority. The escalation culminated in the Bastille's fall two days later.

title: Storming of Bastille
summary: On July 14, 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille while searching for gunpowder and weapons. The fortress held only seven prisoners and had limited strategic value, but its garrison and stores were not wholly irrelevant, and it powerfully symbolised arbitrary royal imprisonment. Governor Bernard-René de Launay and several defenders were killed after the surrender. The victory demonstrated that armed citizens could defeat royal authority; the wider Great Fear that followed also drew on rural rumours, grain insecurity, and fear of aristocratic retaliation.

title: Monarchy Abolished
summary: On September 21, 1792, the newly elected National Convention abolished monarchy and declared France a republic. The decision followed the insurrection of August 10, which had suspended Louis XVI, and the deepening war crisis. The French victory at Valmy on September 20 strengthened confidence that the new political order could survive. The king was put on trial later that year, but royalism and the possibility of restoration did not disappear.

title: Execution of Louis XVI
summary: Louis XVI was guillotined on January 21, 1793 after conviction for conspiracy against public liberty and the security of the state. The execution made compromise with constitutional monarchy far less plausible and intensified hostility between revolutionary France and European monarchies. Britain, the Dutch Republic, and Spain entered the widening war in the following weeks, although military conflict had already begun in 1792. Inside France, royalist resistance continued rather than vanishing with the king.

title: Reign of Terror
summary: From 1793 to 1794, revolutionary government used emergency courts, surveillance, requisitions, and executions while France faced foreign war, civil rebellion, economic crisis, and factional conflict. Revolutionary tribunals issued roughly 16,000–17,000 formal death sentences; broader estimates of 30,000–40,000 deaths include summary executions, prison deaths, and killings in civil war, depending on methodology. Robespierre was highly influential but did not rule alone. He and close allies were arrested on 9 Thermidor and executed the next day.

title: Political Radicalization
summary: The failed constitutional monarchy, the Flight to Varennes, war, the August 1792 insurrection, food shortages, and internal rebellion progressively narrowed the political centre. Girondins and Montagnards were shifting coalitions rather than a simple sequence from moderates to extremists, and both claimed to defend the Revolution. Suspicion of conspiracy and the pressure to demonstrate civic loyalty made compromise increasingly dangerous, helping turn political rivalry into exclusion, arrest, and violence.

title: Seven Years' War
summary: The Seven Years' War (1756–1763) was fought across Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, and South Asia. France lost Canada and much of its strategic position in India, although several commercial settlements were restored under restrictions. The war enlarged the royal debt and damaged France's international prestige. The desire to weaken Britain and recover influence later encouraged French intervention in the American War of Independence.

title: France Backs American Revolution
summary: France supplied covert aid to the American rebels before entering a formal alliance and war against Britain in 1778. The intervention was driven chiefly by strategic rivalry after the Seven Years' War and contributed decisively to American victory. It also cost the French crown around one billion livres and worsened an already serious fiscal problem. American constitutional arguments and the experience of returning officers influenced some French elites, but they did not provide a complete blueprint for 1789.

title: Louis XVI's Weak Leadership
summary: Louis XVI was conscientious and interested in reform, but he proved indecisive under the combined pressure of court politics, privileged institutions, fiscal breakdown, and popular mobilisation. He repeatedly accepted changes and then sought to limit or reverse them, eroding trust among both reformers and conservatives. His inability to reconcile a workable constitutional role with hopes of recovering royal authority became especially damaging after 1789.

title: Necker Dismissed
summary: Louis XVI dismissed the popular finance minister Jacques Necker on July 11, 1789 — just three days before the Bastille fell. Parisians interpreted the dismissal as a signal that the king was planning to use the troops massing around Paris to dissolve the National Assembly by force. The news spread through the city within hours, and crowds began arming themselves that same afternoon.

title: Harvest Failure of 1788
summary: France's 1788 harvest was poor after drought, destructive storms and hail in some regions, and other adverse weather. The severe winter of 1788–1789 then disrupted transport, milling, employment, and food supplies. The crisis was not a uniform nationwide destruction of crops, but it reduced grain availability and helped drive bread prices to politically dangerous levels in 1789.

title: Women's March on Versailles
summary: On October 5–6, 1789, thousands of market women, workers, political activists, and eventually National Guardsmen travelled from Paris to Versailles, demanding bread and political action. Violence at the palace killed royal guards, and the crowd compelled the royal family and National Assembly to move to Paris. The court was not formally imprisoned, but it now operated under intense pressure from the capital, a circumstance that contributed to the royal family's later attempt to flee.

title: Declaration of Rights of Man
summary: Adopted by the National Assembly on August 26, 1789, the Declaration proclaimed natural rights, equality before the law, national sovereignty, liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression. It drew on Enlightenment thought, French political debate, and Atlantic constitutional precedents. It became one of the foundational statements of modern rights-based politics, even though women, enslaved people, and colonial subjects were not granted equal political standing in practice. Later movements invoked, expanded, and contested its universal language.

title: Flight to Varennes
summary: On June 20–21, 1791, Louis XVI and his family attempted to reach the loyalist military stronghold of Montmédy near France's northeastern frontier. They were recognised during the journey and stopped at Varennes before being returned to Paris. Emperor Leopold II was Marie Antoinette's brother, not her nephew, and the plan was not simply a dash across the Austrian border. The attempted flight confirmed suspicions that the king opposed the revolutionary settlement and gravely damaged support for constitutional monarchy.

title: European Coalitions Against France
summary: Austria and Prussia issued the conditional Declaration of Pillnitz in August 1791, hoping partly to deter further threats to the French royal family. Revolutionary France declared war on Austria in April 1792, and Prussia soon joined the conflict. Britain, the Dutch Republic, and Spain entered the wider First Coalition in 1793 after the king's execution and further French expansion. War mobilised support for the Revolution but also deepened division, suspicion, conscription, and emergency government.

title: Thermidorian Reaction
summary: On 9 Thermidor Year II (July 27, 1794), opponents in the National Convention moved against Robespierre, Saint-Just, and their allies, who were executed the next day. The Thermidorian Reaction then curtailed the institutions and laws associated with the Terror over a period of months: the Committee of Public Safety lost authority, the Law of 22 Prairial was repealed, political prisoners were released, and the Jacobin Club was closed. The transition was neither immediate nor peaceful and was followed by reprisals known as the White Terror.

title: The Directory
summary: The Constitution of Year III created a five-member Directory that governed from November 1795 to November 1799. Its divided executive was intended to prevent dictatorship, but the regime faced continuing war, fiscal instability, royalist and neo-Jacobin opposition, and dependence on military force. Directors annulled elections and used coups to preserve the constitutional order. The government was not literally despised by everyone, yet its weak legitimacy and reliance on successful generals made Napoleon's seizure of power possible.

title: Napoleon Seizes Power
summary: Napoleon Bonaparte took power in the coup of 18–19 Brumaire (November 9–10, 1799) with civilian conspirators including Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès and support from key military and political figures. The coup encountered confusion and resistance before a new constitution concentrated authority in the First Consul. Napoleon preserved legal equality for men, many property transfers, administrative centralisation, and careers based partly on talent, while restricting elections, censoring the press, strengthening patriarchal authority, and later restoring slavery in French colonies. The coup ended the Directory and is often used to mark the Revolution's political close.

title: Napoleonic Wars
summary: The wars of Revolutionary and Napoleonic France transformed Europe's borders and institutions. French armies introduced or imposed legal equality, administrative centralisation, secularisation, and the abolition of some corporate privileges in several territories, but they also extracted taxes, manpower, and resources. Occupation generated resistance and helped stimulate competing forms of nationalism. Napoleon's defeat led to the settlements of 1814–1815 and the Concert of Europe, not to a simple restoration of the pre-1789 order.

title: Revolutionary Ideas Spread
summary: The Revolution transformed political vocabulary by making citizenship, equality before the law, popular sovereignty, and the abolition of inherited privilege central questions across the Atlantic world. The Haitian Revolution arose within this connected crisis while exposing the limits of French claims to universal rights. Napoleonic conquest carried some reforms abroad while subordinating other peoples, and later liberal, anticolonial, and national movements drew selectively on revolutionary precedents alongside their own local causes. The Revolution's influence was profound but never uniform or uncontested.

title: Feudalism Abolished in France
summary: During the night of August 4–5, 1789, the National Assembly responded to the Great Fear and rural attacks on seigneurial property by renouncing privileges and approving sweeping reforms. Personal servitudes and several corporate privileges were abolished, but many dues treated as property rights initially remained redeemable through compensation, and the decrees required later clarification and legislation. The revolutionary settlement dismantled the legal order of privilege over several years; complete abolition of remaining seigneurial dues without compensation came only in 1793.
